questions.prompt: You bought contoso.com from a third-party registrar and created a contoso.com zone with records in Azure DNS. Internet lookups still return the old records. What must you do?
options: Create a CNAME at the apex pointing to Azure DNS
At the registrar, set the domain's name servers to the four Azure DNS name servers listed in the zone's NS record
Transfer the domain registration to Azure DNS
Lower the TTL of every record to 60 seconds
questions.explanation: Hosting a domain in Azure DNS requires delegation: the registrar's NS records for the domain must point to Azure's name servers.
why_not: CNAMEs aren't allowed at the apex, and delegation is done with NS records at the registrar.
Azure DNS isn't a registrar; you delegate, you don't transfer.
TTL changes don't move authority to Azure.

questions.prompt: The root domain contoso.com must point to a web app's public IP behind a load balancer, and stay correct if that IP changes. What record should you create?
options: A CNAME at the apex to the load balancer's DNS name
A static A record with the current IP
A TXT record with the IP address
An alias A record at the apex that targets the public IP resource
questions.explanation: Alias records point to Azure resources, update automatically when their IP changes, become empty if the resource is deleted, and work at the apex.
why_not: CNAME records aren't permitted at the zone apex.
It won't follow an IP change and can become a dangling record.
TXT records don't route clients.

questions.prompt: VMs in VNet-A must register their names automatically in internal.contoso.com, and VMs in VNet-B (not peered) must be able to resolve those names. How do you configure the links?
options: Link VNet-A with auto-registration enabled, and link VNet-B as a resolution link
Peer the VNets; private zones resolve only across peerings
Enable auto-registration on both links
Create the zone as a public zone
questions.explanation: A registration link auto-creates A records for that VNet's VMs; resolution links let other VNets query the zone. Peering isn't required for DNS.
why_not: Linked VNets resolve the zone without peering.
That registers VNet-B's VMs too; the requirement only asks VNet-B to resolve.
Public zones can't resolve private addresses for your VNets.

questions.prompt: A VNet uses a custom DNS server running on a VM. VMs can no longer resolve names in a private DNS zone linked to the VNet. What fixes it?
options: Link the zone to the VNet a second time
Enable auto-registration
Configure the custom DNS server to forward queries for the zone to 168.63.129.16, or use Azure DNS Private Resolver
Convert the private zone to a public zone
questions.explanation: With a custom DNS server on the VNet, private zones aren't queried automatically; forward the zone to Azure DNS (168.63.129.16) or use a Private Resolver.
why_not: The link already exists; custom DNS bypasses it.
Registration doesn't change which server answers queries.
That would expose names and still not resolve private IPs.

questions.sub_skill: Configure an internal or public load balancer
questions.prompt: Internet users must reach a web application on port 443 running on three VMs, with failed VMs removed from rotation automatically. What do you deploy?
options: An internal load balancer with HA ports
An inbound NAT rule for each VM
A Standard public load balancer with a backend pool, a health probe and a load-balancing rule for port 443
Three public IPs with a DNS A record set listing all three
questions.explanation: A public load balancer distributes new flows across the backend pool and stops sending them to instances that fail the health probe.
why_not: Internal load balancers have private frontends; HA ports are for NVAs.
NAT rules forward to one specific instance; they don't balance.
DNS round robin doesn't health-check or remove failed VMs.

questions.sub_skill: Configure an internal or public load balancer
questions.prompt: Admins need RDP to one specific VM behind a public load balancer, through the load balancer's IP, on port 50001. What do you configure?
options: An inbound NAT rule mapping frontend port 50001 to port 3389 on that VM
A load-balancing rule for port 3389
An outbound rule
HA ports
questions.explanation: An inbound NAT rule forwards traffic from a frontend IP and port to a specific backend instance.
why_not: A load-balancing rule distributes to all instances, not a specific VM.
Outbound rules provide SNAT for outbound traffic.
HA ports load-balance all ports on internal load balancers.

questions.sub_skill: Configure an internal or public load balancer
questions.prompt: A network virtual appliance pair must receive all TCP and UDP traffic on every port from an internal load balancer. What do you configure?
options: One load-balancing rule per port on a public load balancer
Session persistence set to client IP
A Basic internal load balancer
An HA ports rule (protocol All, port 0) on an internal Standard load balancer
questions.explanation: HA ports load-balance all TCP and UDP flows on all ports of an internal Standard load balancer, typically for NVAs.
why_not: Public load balancers don't support HA ports, and per-port rules are impractical.
Persistence controls stickiness, not port coverage.
Basic is retired and never supported HA ports.

questions.sub_skill: Configure an internal or public load balancer
questions.prompt: A web app behind a load balancer stores session state in memory, so each user must keep reaching the same backend VM. What should you change?
options: Change the health probe to HTTPS
Set the rule's session persistence to Client IP
Add more backend VMs
Use five-tuple distribution
questions.explanation: Session persistence based on client IP (2-tuple) or client IP and protocol (3-tuple) sends a client's flows to the same backend.
why_not: The probe protocol doesn't affect which backend a client reaches.
More backends make stickiness worse, not better.
Five-tuple hashing is the default that spreads a user's flows.

questions.prompt: All backends of a Standard load balancer show as down. The VMs are running and the app listens on the probe port. An NSG on the backend subnet has a rule at priority 200 denying all inbound TCP on that port. What is the cause?
options: The deny rule blocks health probes from 168.63.129.16 before the default AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule (65001) is reached
Standard load balancers don't support NSGs
The probe interval is too short
The backend VMs need public IPs
questions.explanation: Probes come from 168.63.129.16 (the AzureLoadBalancer tag). A higher-priority custom deny blocks them, so backends are marked down.
why_not: NSGs are required for Standard load balancers.
Interval affects detection speed, not success.
Backends don't need public IPs.

questions.prompt: A Standard public load balancer shows all backends healthy in Health Probe Status, but clients time out. Nothing else has changed. What's the most likely cause?
options: The health probe uses the wrong path
The frontend public IP is Basic
No NSG rule allows the client traffic to the backends; Standard load balancers are closed to inbound flows by default
Session persistence is set to None
questions.explanation: Standard is secure by default: inbound flows are closed unless an NSG allows them, separately from probe traffic.
why_not: Probes are healthy, so the probe is configured correctly.
A Standard load balancer requires a Standard public IP; it wouldn't deploy with Basic.
None is the default and doesn't block traffic.

questions.prompt: Which metric tells you whether clients can get through a load balancer's frontend to any healthy backend, rather than each backend's own health?
options: Health Probe Status
SNAT Connection Count
Byte Count
Data Path Availability
questions.explanation: Data Path Availability tests each frontend port with a rule every 25 seconds through to a healthy backend; Health Probe Status measures each backend.
why_not: That measures each backend's probe results, in isolation from the frontend.
It measures outbound SNAT connections.
It measures volume, not availability.

questions.prompt: A backend VM tries to connect to the frontend IP of the internal load balancer it belongs to, and the connection fails, while other VMs reach it fine. Why?
options: Internal load balancers don't support TCP
An outbound flow from a backend VM to its own internal load balancer's frontend isn't supported
The VM's health probe is failing
The VM needs a public IP
questions.explanation: Microsoft lists this limitation: outbound flow from a backend VM to a frontend of an internal load balancer fails.
why_not: They support TCP and UDP.
Other clients reach the frontend fine, so the backends are healthy.
Internal load balancers use private IPs.
